Cannot clearly make out the combinations (try to fit the various forms of energy into the corresponding categories — is it itchy, numb, loose, tight, or hot?)
④
Unable to maintain the purity of the energy (unable to let go of the discriminating views one clings to, unable to observe with a mind of equanimity)
⑤
Unable to bring it out in daily life

Xingxiong thought to himself: “Ah! I suppose I’d be the one stuck at the fourth step. Hmm... at times like this, seeing what has happened as an illusion, or acknowledging that one has created it oneself, actually helps rather a lot!”

The instructor said: “These are all obstacles beginners run into, but it doesn’t matter. As long as you practice more, you’ll naturally improve every day; sooner or later you’ll perfect your wondrous skill, and then you really will be invulnerable to swords and spears!

Some of the students exchanged smiles of understanding, and Xiangdong was likewise full of confidence. This was just to her taste. Though calling upon love and light could indeed bring some comfort to her negative feelings at the time, after all it was still at the level of “always be diligent in wiping it clean”; this Huangting Chan, however, could provide a truly ultimate and fundamental way of liberation.

And Xiangdong also thought that if one were stuck at the fourth step, seeing the external circumstances that robbed one of equanimity as one’s own creation or as illusion was still quite useful — on this point she was of one mind with Xingxiong. For when you understand that this external circumstance may be an illusion, it becomes easier to let go of the emotional attachment that arises in the heart because of that external condition, and to realize that this emotional attachment is nothing but a slight surge of qi and blood!

All right!” the instructor announced, “Now we are about to enter the stage of basic practice!” Seeing the puzzled looks of the students below, the instructor smiled: “The so-called basic practice is exactly the question that classmate just raised — how to strengthen your ability to practice Huangting Chan. The method we use is: sitting meditation.”

The moment Xingxiong heard “sitting meditation” his head throbbed. He was himself like a hyperactive child, unable to sit still for even a few minutes; to make him sit stock-still in place was harder than climbing to heaven. In his ear, the instructor’s words continued: ‘When you sit in meditation, put all your attention on observing the mind; at that time you will experience all kinds of sensations and idle thoughts, and this is the best moment to practice Huangting Chan.’

Seeing the difficulty on Xingxiong’s face, the instructor said considerately: ‘It’s all right — I will guide you gradually. If sitting is uncomfortable you may change your posture.’ Then he turned again to the whole class: ‘You should all know why sitting meditation increases your ability to practice Huangting Chan. Because in the course of sitting, when you feel idle thoughts flying about, or your legs aching and feet numb, you can observe what surge of qi and what churning of blood there is in the Yellow Court, and then practice your equanimity — just observe them purely, without adding any label or thought.’

At this point beautiful, ethereal music sounded in the meditation hall, and the instructor’s deep, steady voice followed: ‘Now we are about to begin the Huangting Chan sitting meditation. You may sit cross-legged in any posture you like, or sit directly on a chair, but do not lean against the back of the chair.’
Xingxiong could only sit there obediently, feeling the helplessness in his own heart.

Minute by minute, time passed; his right leg grew more and more numb, almost beyond endurance. He recalled the instructor’s words: ‘Try not to move. Remember, no one has been hurt merely by sitting a couple of hours in meditation. If it hurts, just look at that pain — look at how deep, how hot, how tight, how sore the most painful point is; look only at its true nature, and do not tack your likes and dislikes onto it.’

Xingxiong was already beginning to grimace a little, and at that moment he truly could feel the upheaval in the Yellow Court. Then he heard the instructor again: ‘Observe whether the sensations in the various parts of the body are at ease — not whether you yourself are at ease.’

That’s strange,” thought Xingxiong. “I’m so ill at ease — can you really be at ease? Hmm, but what if I turn it around and let you be at ease — would I then be at ease?” Xingxiong decided to let his leg be numb to its heart’s content, to see just what would happen. After he made that decision, he discovered that the numbness of the leg truly could exist independently, without having to affect the Yellow Court. Stranger still, when he allowed it to be numb to the full, the sensation of numbness actually vanished; but Xingxiong did not feel pleased by this, because he found that now his back had begun to ache violently — a spot on his back was hurting terribly.

When the sitting meditation ended, Xingxiong had already “shuttled back and forth” between numb legs, aching back, and sore knees many times over, without the least sense that this sitting had actually lasted fifty minutes. Recalling the mixed sweet and bitter experiences of just now, Xingxiong thought, this really is like our life!
Xingxiong feels fear and calm on the steel cables — learning to live with negative emotions)

The next day, on a beautiful Zhongling Mountain morning, Xiangdong stood on the great lawn before the meditation hall and saw great drifts of mist and cloud drifting over from the Emerald Reservoir in the neighboring valley, rolling in like a waterfall — a scene of indescribable beauty. Xiangdong felt truly blessed and happy. Though she knew the road of life is never smooth and free of worry, she had truly already obtained many treasures to carry her safely and without mishap all the way home.
In the following lesson, the instructor took them to an outdoor platform and had them walk the double ropes.

The so-called double ropes are two thick steel cables suspended parallel, one above the other. A person walking them steps on the lower cable with his feet, grasps the upper cable with both hands, and covers a distance of eighty meters, while the highest point of the double ropes is four stories above the ground.

The moment Xingxiong saw it his legs went weak. He did not want to lose face in front of Xiangdong, but he had truly had a fear of heights since childhood... how was he to handle this? The instructor repeatedly assured them that the exercise was very safe, since everyone was strapped into a safety line; even if one lost his footing, at worst one would just end up hanging from the cables. But that was not what Xingxiong feared — he simply had a fear of heights.

They all took turns going up, one after another. The instructor, holding a megaphone, called up to them from below: ‘Turn your observation back to your Yellow Court. See clearly that your fear is nothing but a fluctuation of qi and blood in the chest. Live in peace with it; do not resist, do not suppress, do not shift away, do not take deep breaths — just be well together with it.’

At last it was Xingxiong’s turn. His face was pale, and his hands and feet began to tremble uncontrollably. Even the teaching assistant asked him: ‘Are you all right? Are you sure you want to go up? No need to force yourself.’ As Xingxiong was deliberating, he glanced sideways and saw that Xiangdong had already completed her first round and was walking over happily, preparing to try a second. Xingxiong went up without another thought.

At the very start, Xingxiong crumpled at the starting point, unable to move. The instructor, seeing this from a distance, began his psychological rallying call: ‘Do not stay where you are; move forward. See clearly the true nature of fear, study its physical nature, understand that it is nothing but a vibration of qi and blood. You can do it, Xingxiong — you can live in peace with it.’

Guided all the way by the instructor’s encouragement and support, Xingxiong gritted his teeth and made it to the end. When he came down his whole body was limp, his hands and feet powerless, and his clothing soaked through. Looking up from below, Xingxiong truly could not believe that he had walked the whole distance at that height. Beneath the tyranny of fear, every step he took was extremely slow, but at least he had done it!
The instructor encouraged him: ‘Go on, go a second time. This time, try all the more to recognize its true face, and say to it: “Come on! Come as much as you like!”’

Xingxiong decided to try once more. This time was far better than the last; he truly could look at his own fear and live in peace with it. Not by deep breathing or self-encouragement, not by calling upon light to rescue him — Xingxiong simply dwelt together with fear without prejudice, allowing it to exist, and even bravely said to it: ‘Come on, come as much as you like.’

At a certain point in the middle, Xingxiong suddenly stopped and did not move for a long while, so that a whole crowd behind him was blocked. The instructor waited patiently, but finally could not help asking: ‘Xingxiong, what’s the matter?’
Xingxiong suddenly cried out: ‘How can this be? I feel fear and calm at the same time, and both are present. How very strange!’

On the last stretch, Xingxiong felt that his fear had seemingly become his good friend, always accompanying him; but because Xingxiong no longer resisted it, fear could no longer hinder his actions. Fear was still present — only Xingxiong was no longer afraid of it, and could dwell together with it in peace and mutual ease.
After walking the double ropes twice, Xingxiong felt an indescribable sense of accomplishment. He had truly done it — not by overcoming fear, but by learning to live with it.

The two-day course came to an end. After bidding farewell to the instructor and the volunteer staff, Xingxiong and Xiangdong made their reluctant way down the mountain. Having learned such precious things in this beautiful pure land among the human world, they resolved: “Next time we must come again!”
After seeing Xiangdong off, the first thing Xingxiong did upon returning home was to telephone Xiaofei.
Xiaofei, upon hearing it was him, hesitated a moment. Xingxiong began:

Xiaofei, I am very dissatisfied with your decision.” As he spoke, Xingxiong closely turned his observation back to his own Yellow Court. “I really don’t want the child to go abroad at such a young age, but you are his guardian; you have the right to decide, and I cannot interfere.” Xingxiong himself was surprised that he could say all of it with such composure. Though the Yellow Court swayed now and again, he opened wide his breast and allowed whatever sensations there were to exist.
There was a long silence at the other end of the line, and Xingxiong thought Xiaofei had hung up. ‘Hello! Hello! Are you still there?’

Ahem! I’m still here. Yes, Xingxiong, I was just about to tell you — I’ve thought it over, and the child indeed is still young; perhaps when he reaches middle school or high school we can discuss this matter again.”

After hanging up, Xingxiong could not help jumping and laughing again and again, and then, out of habit, he turned his observation back to the Yellow Court and found the qi and blood churning ceaselessly within, along with a ticklish, tingling sensation. Heh heh, this Yellow Court! Xingxiong shook his head.
— The Ultimate Wondrous Remedy for Emotional Liberation

Six years ago I sank to a low point in life. My feeling was: all the pursuit of external things is hollow, and cannot give me final satisfaction. What was I to do? And so I took the path of spiritual growth and seeking within.

Over these past years I have read through books in both Chinese and English, and sought out famous teachers in many places around the world, learning all sorts of methods of spiritual growth. When I came to write Meeting the Unknown Self, I felt I had found a clear path, and so decided to share this map of spiritual practice with everyone.

But when I kept practicing, I felt my spiritual map was still missing a piece. I had many doubts, and no teacher able to answer them. Though both my spiritual and material life had greatly improved, I still felt that what I had learned was not an ultimate, fundamental path.

Moreover, while studying abroad I saw Westerners discoursing at length on our Eastern philosophy; in India, foreigners earnestly studied India’s spiritual practices. On the mainland and in Taiwan, many fine teachers were foreigners, and we had to study under them through interpreters. Even when at great effort I found a good teacher who spoke Chinese, the things he knew had all been learned abroad.

I could not help asking: where has our Chinese culture of five thousand years gone? Why did our ancestors not speak of spiritual practice, but only of an empty, vacuous cultivation of quiescence (what I took to be Daoism and Laozi), or of the stereotyped benevolence, righteousness, and morality of the eight-legged essay (what I took to be Confucianism)? Or else Buddhism, whose source is likewise India, and which at times is truly a little deep, carrying a strong religious coloring — not everyone can accept it.

On this trip to Taiwan I chanced to see a Spring Festival meditation retreat at a Chan temple, in the Xindian mountain area not far from the outskirts of Taipei, with beautiful scenery and no fee at all. The teacher looked solemn and respectable (I am very particular about the appearance and spirit of spiritual teachers). With the mood of a vacation, and wishing to strengthen my own sitting practice by means of group meditation, I signed up with my husband for a three-day closed retreat in Huangting Chan.

At the time I thought: I’ve heard about and learned a great deal about meditation — what could be so special? What is Huangting Chan? I’d never even heard of it, so I might as well go and have a bit of fun. I never expected that after the three days of classes I would truly feel, “Seeking it a thousand times in the crowd, then turning suddenly to look — and there it is, in my old home of Taiwan!” Heh heh! Zhang Qingxiang, the founder of Huangting Chan, is the same age as me, but with a very old soul. The meditative method he teaches is the best I have ever seen. Through him I at last understood what the true purpose of sitting in meditation really is. In time I will share it all gradually with everyone.

This Teacher Zhang’s learning and cultivation are truly profound. He is thoroughly versed in the various classics of the three teachings (Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism), so that when he speaks he quotes the classics and scriptures, laying out everything methodically and convincingly. Still, I have seen many such people. Whether one truly practices or not, I in fact know at a glance. Yet the way the teacher expounded the Four Books and Five Classics filled me with admiration. The conventional moral essays (such as the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean), under his interpretation, turned out to be charged with extremely profound spiritual meaning, which delighted me beyond measure. It turned out that our ancestors really were masters of spiritual practice, of a very high plane — so high that later generations cannot immediately comprehend its true meaning. Ah! How wonderful! (Perhaps that was my own prejudice and ignorance of the past!)

The “Huangting Chan” that Teacher Zhang created himself is a practical method he realized through studying ancient texts — and it is the last piece of my spiritual map: especially practical, highly operable, clear and plain. Over the three days of the course, my husband and I continuously used the method the teacher taught to realize the states that the author of The Power of Now describes. I had read of these states before in books, but putting them into practice was truly difficult. The method Teacher Zhang provided made up for this deficiency.

Furthermore, I have attended many spiritual classes, but many teachers are not the sort you can approach casually; once class is over they disappear. But Teacher Zhang is available at any time. His patience and sincerity are truly moving. He has not the slightest air of authority; he is sincere, plain, and will answer any question at all, and his face always bears a trace of a smile that makes one feel at ease at the sight. He calls himself “instructor” and has us call him instructor as well — truly humble and sincere. I had accumulated a great heap of questions about practice, which previously I could either find no one to ask, or the teachers’ answers left me unsatisfied; and this time I truly asked them all in one go, and Teacher Zhang’s answers all convinced me.

For example, when I sit in meditation my thoughts are always flying in all directions, which troubled me for a long time; that is why each time I could only sit half an hour, and could not enter concentration. (Yes, even though I could lead group meditation, my own skill was not yet up to par. But after the three-day retreat, sitting for an hour and twenty minutes is no longer any problem at all. This was something that had never happened in any meditation retreat I had attended before.)

I asked many teachers how to deal with scattered thoughts. Their answers were: ‘That’s fine, just let the thoughts fly; as soon as you notice, bring them back.’ (Yes, that is what I did, and I have taught others to do it too — but it wears one out. How long must I keep battling my thoughts?) ‘Ask yourself: who is thinking?’ (That does not work either; I would say Defen is thinking, and so what?) ‘Be an observer; observe your thoughts coming and going.’ (So what if I watch? It’s still fretful! There are still so many thoughts!)

There was also an Indian guru who held: the state of “no-thought” is only the beginning of the meditative state, not yet true meditation. Hearing this at the time I thought: then I’m finished! I would probably have to cultivate for ten lifetimes before entering no-thought. This guru suggested listening to CDs of his lectures (in Hindi) or praying to him to gain the state of no-thought; and I tried that too, but it still did not work.

Teacher Zhang’s answer, however, was quite wonderful. He said that the head is by nature made for thinking, just as the eyes are made for seeing. So when one sits down, it is perfectly normal that the head thinks. What matters is to notice whether one has idle thoughts — that is, the deluded thoughts that give rise to negative reactions — and these are to be removed. So no-thought does not mean having no thoughts, but having no idle thoughts. (Brilliant, right? It was a great liberation for me!)

And Teacher Zhang further pointed out that you have many thoughts, especially idle thoughts, because there is a certain negative emotion sustaining them. For instance, if you are anxious, you will keep scheming about the future; if you are sad, you will keep returning to the past to relive the matter that broke your heart. So what matters is how to deal with the emotion, not how to deal with the thinking. The method for dealing with emotion that Teacher Zhang taught (which is precisely Huangting Chan!) is the most effective, the most reasonable, and the most helpful of any I have seen!

When I first set out on the path of spiritual growth, most of the reason was due to affliction by emotions. After years of research and searching, I discovered that the ways people generally deal with emotion can be divided into two broad categories:

1. Denial, avoidance, and rationalization (such people generally are not likely to take the path of self-examination and inner contemplation, because their reason is too strong and can persuade themselves.)

2. Expression, deflection, and elimination (such people generally enter the path of religion and spiritual practice, because they acknowledge the existence of their emotions, and gradually come to know that none of these methods above are yet the true way of liberation.)

The methods above are precisely what Shenxiu, the great disciple of the Fifth Patriarch of Chan, called “always be diligent in wiping it clean” — earnestly sweeping out the chambers of one’s heart, clearing away each speck of dust the moment it falls. There is nothing wrong with doing this, but you will be very busy, and after a while you will fling down the cloth and say, ‘What is going on — will the dust never finish being swept away? I have taken so many courses, learned so many things, read so many books, and swept with all earnestness — why does it seem I can never be freed from negative emotions?’

This is the very situation I passed through along the way. Later I read The Power of Now, and was amazed by it as a heavenly book, thinking the method it provides was the ultimate, fundamental method. For my own experience, too, was that the ultimate great method of spiritual growth and liberation from affliction is inner contemplation: turning inward to observe the arising of one’s own thoughts and intentions. This I have said many times before in my earlier blog posts.

The author of The Power of Now mentions an important concept: surrender. Whenever something goes against one’s wishes, if we have learned to surrender, our emotions will not stir up too many waves. (This single skill alone is enough to keep us practicing for a long time.) But later I found that not every matter allows you to surrender. Some things strike us so hard, or are directly connected with our past wounds, that surrender then becomes impossible. So the author says, ‘If you cannot surrender to the event, then surrender to the negative emotion you have raised about it.’ I thought this very reasonable; when I took part in Master Christopher’s workshop, this method was also confirmed. I likewise believe that accepting the present emotion is the ultimate, fundamental method of freeing oneself from emotion.

But as everyone knows, in actual life, when emotion comes we really are powerless before it. To observe it, how does one observe it? To accept it, how does one accept it? We naturally used a few methods too, such as bringing the breath to the place in the body that is uncomfortable, using breath to smooth over that uncomfortable sensation, or calling upon light and love to help us accept it. Yet in truth these methods are still at the level of “always be diligent in wiping it clean,” are they not? So no matter how good these methods are, they always leave me with the feeling of scratching an itch through a boot, as though not striking at the very heart of the matter!

Only when I learned Huangting Chan did I know there is still an ultimate, fundamental method that can help us be liberated. The methods spoken of earlier, if they can resolve your problem in the present moment, may still be used. But what I learned in Huangting Chan is truly the state the Sixth Patriarch spoke of: “Originally there is not a single thing — where could dust alight?”

Zhang Qingxiang, the instructor of Huangting Chan, likewise, moved by the fact that after many years of practice he still could not overcome the problem of emotion, finally discovered after reading all through the ancient classics of our ancestors what all the various schools and sects mean by “cultivating the mind,” and found a genuinely operable method to share with everyone. (A great deed of merit, Teacher!)

Instructor Zhang discovered that whenever we have negative emotions, though the bodily sensations may differ from person to person (some get headaches, some pain in the shoulders or back, a tightness here and a tightness there), there is always a great surge of qi and blood at that square inch at the very center of the chest (which is the danzhong acupoint in Chinese medicine, what we commonly call the heart chakra). After comparing with ancient texts, he found that the place our ancestors called the “Yellow Court” is the very root of what stirs the human heart.

In the meditation classes he taught, we did not merely sit silently; rather, the instructor led us, using all sorts of dynamic methods, to experience our own Yellow Court. The efforts of my past many years had not been wasted. In the classroom I immediately realized that when a thought or intention arising in the present moment stirred my negative emotions, there would be a churning of energy at the very center of the chest (between the two breasts), and the feeling was far from pleasant.

The most interesting thing is that the instructor let us see that though you think you are angry at your husband, though you think it is another’s behavior or an external circumstance that makes you angry, what we truly resist is that surge of qi that is stirred up in the Yellow Court in the chest. Study it closely, and it is nothing more than a little churning of qi and blood, a change in energy. But every time this familiar discomfort rises, we want to curse, to shed tears, or to flee.

The instructor further pointed out that if you study the subtle rise and fall of qi and blood in that square inch of the heart, you will find its physical nature: hot, cold, swelling, contracting, tight, itchy, sore, numb, and so on. Those who have studied quantum physics can also confirm that these changes in energy are nothing but the fluctuations of particles (the smallest elements composing matter) coming and going, and in themselves bear no meaning at all. This is the meaning of the Heart Sutra’s saying, “Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form.”

The amusing thing is that since childhood we have formed a certain clinging and attachment to the rise and fall of qi and blood in our chests — that is, we love and hate and judge it. For instance, when you are angry, you feel the chest is very hot and stuffy and the breath hurried; so what you truly resist and do not accept is not the external circumstance or the other person that caused the rise and fall of your qi and blood, but the sensation on your own body. Where is the proof? Because after you have run a few kilometers, the sensations in your body can be said to be the very same as the angry ones above: hurried breath, boiling blood. Yet not only do you not take offense, you feel great — the “high” (exhilaration) after exercise. And if we were to go to the front line to fight today, the same bodily sensations would arise, and we would interpret them as “courage” — would we not?

So the origin of our afflictions lies in having a mind of greed, anger, and discrimination toward that rise and fall of qi and blood in the square inch at the center of the chest. The instructor’s earnest and repeated teaching, and the various activities designed in the course, all serve to make us perceive what the essence of negative emotions truly is. If we see clearly its emptiness (coming and going beyond our control, and bearing no substantial meaning), we can dwell harmoniously with it when it arises. And the Huangting Chan sitting meditation the instructor teaches is the best method for observing oneself. Under the teacher’s guidance, I went from being unable to sit still for even half an hour to being able at once to sit for more than an hour without changing color. I shall selflessly share these wondrous skills with everyone in time — please wait patiently.

Reaching this point, readers should understand why I consider it the last piece of the puzzle I had always been seeking. The instructor pointed out that the ultimate aim is not to eliminate your emotions (the diligent wiping), but to be able to roam freely and at ease, watching them amid the rise and fall of all kinds of emotions. So you may be raging furiously and cursing at some moment, yet your heart is calm and at ease inside, because you are not afraid of the inner boiling of blood and the churning energy in the chest. And you judge that in the present state, becoming angry is the best way to resolve matters. (Many bosses will know this, right? Heh heh.) So you calmly choose to become angry, rather than being driven into anger because the energy in your heart is stirred beyond your control. Here, you have a choice. You become the master of your own emotions, and no longer their slave. This is liberation from emotion — not the absence of emotion, but living in peace with it. This is also the essence of non-doing (wuwei).
What a wonderful practical method! In days to come I will share more of my insights and realizations with everyone.
